newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM lashes own Finance Ministry over scandals.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM lashes own Finance Ministry over scandals.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, angered by a string of business scandals, lashed out at his own Finance Ministry on Thursday for failing to at least head one of them off.

The wave of scandals has broken in the middle of a campaign by Hashimoto's government to clean up the country's business ethics ahead of "Big Bang" deregulation of its financial markets to make them globally competitive.

In an unusual public rebuke to the country's most powerful bureaucrats, Hashimoto took them to task for not knowing that the country's third-largest commercial bank, Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank, might be involved in questionable loans to a racketeer.
"It's not only a matter of Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank. There must have been inspections by the Finance Ministry," Hashimoto told reporters.
He also did not spare top executives of the bank, decrying reports that they might resign over the affair as "sneaky".

"It's sneaky (for the DKB leadership) to step down to take the blame," Hashimoto said. "Their resigning does not settle the problem. They should face up to the case until investigations make headway."

Media reports have said DKB chairman Tadashi Okuda, president Katsuhiko Kondo and other top current and former executives are expected to quit over links to a scandal also involving the country's largest brokerage, Nomura Securities Co.

At the heart of the affair is the activities of a "sokaiya" or racketeer who prosecutors suspect was given financial favours by both companies to stop him disrupting their shareholders' meetings by asking sensitive business questions.
Japan's Commercial Code bans companies from making payments to sokaiya.
There were two new blows to Japan's business image on Thursday.

The Finance Ministry banned Nikko Securities Investment Trust and Management Co, an affiliate of leading brokerage Nikko Securities Co Ltd, from establishing new trust funds for one month from June 2 because of illegal bond trading.

"It is truly regrettable that such illegal acts were conducted at Nikko Securities Investment Trust and Management Co," Atsushi Nagano, director-general of the Finance Ministry's Securities Bureau, said in a statement.

In another case in which there was no suggestion of wrongdoing, the Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd (IBJ), a blue blood among Japanese banks, said its London branch made a 10 billion yen ($86.9 million) loss from derivatives trading as of April 1.

An IBJ spokesman said there had been no wrongdoing and that the bank did not have any risk management problems from losses that were on the branch's entire derivatives portfolio and did not result from any one individual transaction.
Hangovers from two old scandals were also in the headlines.
The president of top department store operator Takashimaya Co apologised to shareholders for a scandal also involving a sokaiya that resulted in the arrests of four Takashimaya executives last June.

Giant trading house Sumitomo Corp, falling into the red in the year that ended in March for the first time ever due to the hefty trading losses blamed on its former star copper trader, announced it will cut summer bonuses for not only executives but all employees.
The total value of the cuts is two billion yen ($17.3 million), the company said in a statement.
